pendingReview.title: As package thefts plagued a Princeton apartment complex, grad students took matters into their own hands
pendingReview.description: Binoculars, life-saving medication, speakers, designer perfumes, bagged groceries, raincoats, and blackout curtains have all gone missing in a spree of alleged package thefts that have rattled the Meadows Apartments, a Princeton-owned graduate student housing complex. From the beginning of July to the end of September 2026, 56 thefts were reported at the Meadows Apartments, according to the Department of Public Safety's daily crime logs - making up over half of the 108 total on-campus thefts reported over the same period. Only two thefts were reported from July to September at the other two graduate student apartment complexes, Lawrence and Lakeside. The sheer volume and frequency of missing packages even pushed two graduate students to take matters into their own hands in mid-August and attempt to capture video evidence about the packages going missing. Following the installation of an official security camera in the Meadows package room in late August, reported thefts at the apartment complex have decreased significantly. According to University spokesperson Michael Hotchkiss, Amazon lockers are also set to be installed during the fall semester to help prevent theft of Amazon packages. The University did not directly comment on multiple questions related to the string of thefts at Meadows. Jungwoo Lee GS told The Daily Princetonian that his package went missing in July after Amazon marked it as delivered to the Meadows Apartments package room. He didn't think much about it and promptly requested a refund from Amazon. But when Lee's packages went missing five times in a row, "Amazon thought that I was a scammer who kept asking [for] the refund, so they blocked my account," Lee said. "So I don't have an Amazon account right now." Lee is one of dozens of graduate students who have reported or raised concerns to PSafe and University officials about delivered packages going missing in or around the Meadows package room. According to over 100 messages sent in the Graduate Student Slack channel reviewed by the 'Prince,' messages such as 'Has anyone seen this package in the mailroom?' and 'If someone took my package by mistake, please put it back' peppered the channel nearly every week from June to September. Despite repeated calls for tighter security measures, many Meadows residents told the 'Prince' that they have seen delayed or insufficient action from University officials and PSafe amid the months-long string of alleged thefts they said have agitated their residential community. "We have been working closely with Public Safety, Housing, and residents to address the matter appropriately and in accordance with University policies," Lily Secora, Associate Dean for Student Affairs at the Graduate School, wrote in a statement to the 'Prince.' But students like Donaldson Larbie GS are frustrated with "the sheer frequency" of package thefts in and around the apartment complex. This string of thefts, Larbie said, "is like every day, and everybody is complaining about the same issue, so it can't just be a coincidence." Lax security and mounting thefts Graduate students described instances of package thefts at Meadows dating back to 2024, when the apartment complex first opened across Lake Carnegie. The apartment complex has 379 housing units for graduate students and their families and houses several athletic facilities. For the 2026-2027 academic year, a studio room in Meadows costs $1,294 to $1,317 per bed per month, and a one-bedroom arrangement costs between $1,726 and $1,819. Over the years, the accessibility of the package room and a lack of cameras or a full-time package organizer in the room has been a long-standing security issue, multiple graduate students told the 'Prince.' Unlike their sister housing complex, Lawrence Apartments, Meadows and Lakeside Apartments are managed by American Campus Communities, not the University. Whenever students petitioned for a camera in the locker room, they said they were told that PSafe can only install cameras on or near University-managed buildings. Multiple PSafe personnel did not respond directly to requests for comment from the 'Prince.' "Housing, the Graduate School and Public Safety have been in conversation with residents of Lawrence, Lakeside and Meadows for some time about package delivery, handling and theft concerns," Hotchkiss wrote to the 'Prince.' Hotchkiss added that concerns have been addressed in a variety of ways, including the option for high-value items to be delivered to Frist Campus Center - 1.1 miles away from Meadows. However, as of Nov. 4, the entrances to the building that the package room is located in are accessible during the day without a University ID, and the actual package room has no door separating it from the hallway. When the 'Prince' visited the room in November, packages too large to fit in the medium-sized lockers were strewn about the room or placed in openly accessible bins. Among the packages were brightly colored posters and notices warning Meadows residents against potential package thefts. These security vulnerabilities have led to a string of reported thefts ranging from food to dishware, students said. But in other cases, the missing packages carried far greater consequences. One second-year Ph.D. student, who requested anonymity due to security and privacy concerns, had Skyrizi, a roughly $24,000 medical injection, go missing in mid-August despite receiving a photograph of it being delivered to the Meadows package room. The injection helps patients achieve remission in chronic illnesses. They spent the next half of their work week making phone calls to get a replacement. In total, they estimate about 20 hours of phone calls between physicians, insurance, the medical device manufacturers, the company that sends them the medical devices, UPS, and Meadows. Over a week later, the student finally got their replacement device, but is no longer sending their medication to Meadows. Instead, they will send it to a relative who lives out-of-state and pick it up from there every few weeks. "Nobody will advocate for you," the student said. "You have to go in and advocate for yourself every step of the way." While graduate students have the option of shipping valuable packages to Frist Campus Center, packages sent to Meadows, Lawrence, or Lakeside Apartments "are shipped directly to those locations and are not processed for campus distribution via Package and Mail Services," University spokesperson Ahmad Rizvi wrote in a statement to the 'Prince.' According to Rizvi, if a graduate student resident suspects a package was lost or stolen, "the intended recipient should work directly with the courier or shipper, as well as file a report with DPS if the package is suspected stolen," referring to PSafe. Taking matters into their own hands After weeks of submitting reports and seeing little change, two students decided to take matters into their own hands. Susie Song GS had five packages go missing in six weeks, and another graduate student, who requested anonymity for job-related reasons, had lost four in three days. On Aug. 17, the two students placed a fake package containing dog toys and an Apple AirTag in the Meadows package room, alongside setting up a hidden camera in the room with the goal of catching concrete evidence of theft that could be presented to DPS. Within two hours of setting it up, their fake package was gone. They immediately contacted PSafe and showed them the footage after the person of interest had left. The AirTag tracked the package to an apartment in Meadows, and they were able to identify the student who took their package through word of mouth. The person of interest claimed that the AirTag had fallen out of the package and that it was a mistake, according to students who set the camera up. The students also presented their findings to PSafe and received an email from PSafe Detective Alvan Flanders the following morning asking them to meet. At the meeting, they were discouraged from getting involved any further, the students said. Flanders did not respond to multiple requests for comment. They were notified on Aug. 19 that an investigation was officially open, yet 10 days later on Aug. 29, they were told by PSafe that there was nothing they could do, and that they would have to go through the West Windsor Municipal Court if the students wanted to continue pursuing the case. However, since the incident occurred on campus, the officers at West Windsor said that these matters were within PSafe's jurisdiction, according to the students. Detective Lieutenant William Jones of the West Windsor Township Police Department confirmed in an email to the 'Prince' that DPS has the primary responsibility for package theft reports and investigations in the Meadows complex. "The West Windsor Police Department would step in and assist with these investigations at the request of Public Safety after the initial reports have been taken," Jones wrote. After weeks of silence from the University and PSafe, the two students were asked to meet with Shawn Copeland, assistant director of student affairs and residential life at the Graduate School, in mid-September, where they were informed that they violated the University's Recording Policy, they said. They later faced disciplinary action - Song got a reprimand, while the other student was placed on a three-month probation - for violating the policy, which went into effect in January and prohibits audio or video recordings without community members' "knowledge and consent when privacy is reasonably expected." Hotchkiss did not comment directly on the disciplinary measures the University took pursuant to the violation of the University Recording Policy, which was not present in the University's rules handbook; Rights, Rules, Responsibilities; at the time of the incident. Repeated calls for action went unanswered, students say PSafe has made multiple efforts to curb the number of missing packages and encouraged graduate students to submit theft reports. "Public Safety has increased patrols in and around the property. Residents are strongly encouraged to report stolen or missing packages to Public Safety so they can document incidents, investigate, and adjust patrols as needed," a mid-August email notice from American Campus Communities to Meadows residents obtained by the 'Prince' read. PSafe also hosted a two-hour-long tabling session on Sept. 3 at the apartment complex to answer resident questions, including those about missing packages. But students said that they repeatedly urged PSafe, the University, and American Campus Communities to implement additional security in the package room, only to see limited action. American Campus Communities referred the 'Prince' to University Media Relations and did not address questions related to the string of alleged thefts. Chair of the Meadows Apartment Committee, the representative body for Meadows residents, Courteney Malin GS, deferred requests for comment to other members of the graduate student community. As thefts continued throughout August and September, students said that their trust in existing reporting systems faltered. Lee never ended up reporting any of his five missing packages to PSafe. When an anniversary gift for his girlfriend went missing last year with the package wrapping found tossed in the trash, he filed a report with PSafe and provided a suspect of interest. But nothing ever came of it, according to Lee. "I kind of lost my trust in the DPS," Lee said. "I was thinking, Public Safety doesn't care [about] this kind of thing that much. They don't try to take serious action, so I just decided not to do much." Several graduate students expressed similar concerns, with some saying that they had chosen not to report missing packages as they doubted the extent of PSafe's capabilities. These accounts suggest that the number of thefts recorded in PSafe's daily crime logs may not fully reflect the extent of the thefts Meadows residents say they have been experiencing. Chandler Stevenson GS also did not report any of his missing packages to DPS, although many of his friends did. "When I had heard of their experiences with DPS, I think I was rather unmotivated to call the hotline to talk to DPS rather than just going through the channel that I ordered the thing from in the first place and trying to see if I could get another shipment of it," Stevenson said in an interview with the 'Prince.' Increased security measures come to Meadows In October, only one theft at Meadows was reported to PSafe, according to DPS's daily crime logs. "I was not expecting this issue to ever have any kind of resolution," Logan Klinger GS said. "I thought it would just be an issue Meadows residents would have to deal with forever." Klinger previously lived in Meadows but quickly moved out due to a variety of reasons, one of which being package thefts. He now lives in the Lawrence complex and has not had any packages go missing. According to Hotchkiss, the University is currently completing "final local regulatory approvals" for the Amazon lockers at Meadows, Lawrence, and Lakeside. These lockers are expected to become operational during the fall semester and are meant to provide more secure storage of Amazon packages, the majority of deliveries, Hotchkiss wrote. However, some students pointed to a broader culture of theft on campus and in residential areas, which they said discourages any reporting or hope for change. "It's just safe until someone realizes that it's safe, and then they can exploit the vulnerability," the aforementioned anonymous graduate student told the 'Prince.' "I think the default is to not report," they continued. "Because you don't really believe that anything will become of it. We just live in an abnormal culture of theft, but that is our reality." Elizabeth Hu is a senior News writer, assistant head Copy editor, associate Data editor, staff Podcast producer, and contributing Features writer from Houston. She can be reached at exh[at]dailyprincetonian.com. Please send any corrections to corrections[at]dailyprincetonian.com. pendingReview.title: Report: 3 UA Students Sue Tuscaloosa Restaurant Over Ex-Employee's Hidden Restroom Camera
pendingReview.description: Three University of Alabama students have sued a downtown Tuscaloosa restaurant and one of its former employees, alleging the man hid a phone in the restroom and recorded them. The employee, a 30-year-old man named Isabel Mendoza Perez, was arrested in April and has since been indicted on three counts of first-degree voyeurism. Arrested in April According to an April deposition, Tuscaloosa Police believe Mendoza Perez started a video recording on his iPhone inside the women's restroom at Jalapeños on 23rd Avenue on the evening of April 27. He placed the phone in a potted plant with the camera facing the toilet, then moved parts of the plant to hide it and left, the deposition says. It recorded for more than an hour. A young woman using the restroom found the phone still recording, the deposition says. She reviewed the video, deleted it, told management and called police. Officers identified the phone as belonging to Mendoza Perez, an employee of the business, who reportedly told them he had dropped it while changing a light bulb. The deposition says Mendoza Perez gave officers permission to search the phone and unlocked it for them. Officers recovered the deleted video, which included footage of two more women who also wanted to pursue charges. The deposition says officers also found numerous images of nude women on the phone. First-degree voyeurism is a Class C felony under Alabama law. Mendoza Perez has been arrested and indicted by a circuit court, but has not been convicted or pled guilty. The Lawsuit The civil suit was filed in Tuscaloosa County Circuit Court by Birmingham attorneys Freddy Rubio and Jason Yearout of Rubio Law Firm, according to reporting by AL.com. The Thread has not been able to obtain a copy of the complaint. A search of the state's online court records system does not return the case, which can indicate a file has been sealed or marked confidential. AL.com reported the suit names both the restaurant and Mendoza Perez, and argues the restaurant failed in its duty to exercise reasonable care in hiring, training and supervising employees who come into contact with customers. It brings claims including negligent hiring and retention, invasion of privacy, negligence, wantonness and intentional infliction of emotional distress, and seeks unspecified compensatory and punitive damages. The suit also alleges the restaurant's manager pressed the student to hand the phone over to him rather than to police, AL.com reported. Restaurant Cooperating with Police, Blame "Rogue Employee" Trip Umbach, a Birmingham attorney representing Jalapeños, provided a statement to the Thread on the restaurant's behalf. "We take this matter very seriously. The individual was terminated and has not worked in our restaurant since the night of the incident," Umbach said. "Fortunately, these young women were aware of their surroundings and acted vigilantly to protect each other. Their actions prevented the video from being seen by anyone, and they should be commended for how they reacted." "We want to be clear. These were unacceptable actions by a rogue employee and do not reflect our standards or values," he said. "We will continue to cooperate with law enforcement in every way possible, and we remain committed to the safety, privacy, and trust of our customers." For more exclusive coverage of courts and crime in West Alabama, stay connected to the Tuscaloosa Thread.

pendingReview.title: Tuscaloosa Mexican restaurant responds after Alabama students say they were filmed in restroom
pendingReview.description: The attorney for the owners of a Tuscaloosa restaurant that is being sued after an employee secretly filmed women while they were using the bathroom said they take the matter seriously and have fully cooperated with law enforcement. Birmingham attorney Trip Umbach, who represents Jalapenos Downtown Cocina & Tequila Room in a lawsuit filed by the three University of Alabama students, released this statement on behalf of the owners: "The individual was terminated and has not worked in our restaurant since the night of the incident," according to the statement. "Fortunately, these young women were aware of their surroundings and acted vigilantly to protect each other," it continued. "Their actions prevented the video from being seen by anyone, and they should be commended for how they reacted." "We want to be clear. These were unacceptable actions by a rogue employee and do not reflect our standards or values. We will continue to cooperate with law enforcement in every way possible, and we remain committed to the safety, privacy, and trust of our customers." The employee, 31-year-old Isabel Mendoza Perez, has been indicted on three counts of first-degree voyeurism. According to the lawsuit filed in Tuscaloosa Circuit Court by attorneys Freddy Rubio and Jason Yearout, the students went to the restaurant on April 27 to have dinner during the week of final exams. After they finished and paid their bill, they each used a single-occupancy bathroom. Inside that bathroom, one of the students found a cell phone hidden behind a potted plant and aimed directly at the toilet of a single-occupancy bathroom that had been recording women for an hour and a half. "The phone belonged to a Jalapenos employee," said Birmingham attorney Freddy Rubio. "When its video was recovered, it captured one woman after another in the must private moment imaginable, each of them unaware that a stranger was watching and recording them." When the police arrived, Mendoza told officers his phone had fallen while he was changing a lightbulb. The lawsuit states that the video showed Mendoza setting up and concealing the camera, and then a succession of unsuspecting women - including the three UA students - entering the restroom, lowering their clothing and using the restroom. "On the same phone," the lawyers wrote, "officers observed numerous photographs of naked women." The lawsuit alleges that Jalapenos hired Mendoza, assigned him duties that place him in and around the restaurant's restrooms, and gave him unsupervised access to patrols and to the private areas of its premises. "On information and belief, Mendoza was not lawfully authorized to work in the United States," the lawsuit states. "Jalapenos hired and employed him anyway." "Because Jalapenos deliberately avoided the verification and screening that federal and Alabama law require - and that ordinary care independently demanded - it hired a man whose true identity, history and fitness it had never confirmed, could not vouch for and about whom knew essentially nothing," lawyers wrote. "On information and belief, before April 27, 2026, Mendoza had engaged in similar misconduct or exhibited behavior that rendered him unfit to have unsupervised access to Jalapenos patrons," the suit states, "and Jalapenos knew, or in the exercise of due and proper diligence would have learned, of facts giving it notice of the risk he posed." The lawsuit accuses the restaurant and/ or Mendoza of the following: negligent hiring, training, supervision and retention, invasion of privacy, negligence, wantonness, intentional infliction of emotional distress, breach of fiduciary duty, among other claims. The suit is seeking unspecified compensatory and punitive damages.
